content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Define cell differentiation and explain why it occurs
Describe the structure and function of specialised animal cells
Describe the structure and function of specialised plant cells
Explain how the structure of each specialised cell relates to its function
Not all cells in a multicellular organism are the same. Cells become
(or differentiated) to perform specific functions. This process is called
. Specialised cells have specific structural features (adaptations) that enable them to carry out their particular function efficiently.
is the process by which a cell changes to become specialised for its function.
In animals, most differentiation occurs during early development
In plants, differentiation can occur throughout life
All specialised cells originate from unspecialised
During differentiation, certain genes are switched on and others are switched off
Transmit electrical impulses around the body

attrs.alt: Motor neurone showing cell body, dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, and axon terminals

content.text: Increase surface area to connect with other neurones
Insulates the axon and speeds up impulse transmission
Connect to other neurones or effectors
Provide energy (ATP) for active transport of ions
Transport oxygen from the lungs to all body cells

attrs.alt: Red blood cell showing biconcave disc shape, front view and side view

content.text: Increases surface area for gas exchange
Binds to oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin

In the lungs: reaction goes forward (oxygen binds)
In tissues: reaction goes backward (oxygen released)

attrs.alt: Sperm cell showing acrosome, nucleus, midpiece with mitochondria, and tail/flagellum

content.text: Contains enzymes to penetrate the egg
Propels the sperm towards the egg
Be fertilised by sperm and develop into an embryo

attrs.alt: Egg cell showing cell membrane, jelly coat, cytoplasm with food reserves, and nucleus

content.text: Contains food reserves (yolk) for early embryo development
Protects the cell and hardens after fertilisation to prevent multiple fertilisation
Contains 23 chromosomes to combine with sperm
Provides energy for cell division after fertilisation

attrs.alt: Muscle fibre showing multiple nuclei, mitochondria, and protein filaments

content.text: Slide past each other to cause contraction
Control protein production for the large cell
Move mucus and trapped particles (e.g., in airways)

attrs.alt: Ciliated epithelial cells showing cilia on surface and goblet cells between them

content.text: Wave in coordinated motion to move mucus
Allows cilia to beat above the cell surface
Goblet cells produce mucus that traps particles
Absorb water and mineral ions from the soil

attrs.alt: Root hair cell showing hair-like extension, vacuole, and position in root epidermis

content.text: Greatly increases surface area for absorption
Maintains water potential gradient for osmosis
Provide ATP for active transport of mineral ions
Transport water and dissolved minerals up the plant; provide structural support

attrs.alt: Xylem vessel showing hollow tube, lignified walls, and pits

content.text: Hollow tube for unobstructed water flow
Provides strength and prevents collapse; waterproof
Allow water to move sideways to other cells
Transport dissolved sugars (sucrose) and amino acids around the plant

attrs.alt: Phloem showing sieve tube elements and companion cells

content.text: Allow sugars to flow between cells
Provide ATP and proteins for the sieve tube
Main site of photosynthesis in the leaf

attrs.alt: Palisade cell showing many chloroplasts arranged near cell walls

content.text: Packed closely together; more cells per area
Control the opening and closing of stomata for gas exchange and water loss

attrs.alt: Pair of guard cells showing stoma opening, thick inner walls, and chloroplasts

content.text: Thick inner wall, thin outer wall
Cell curves when turgid, opening the stoma
Produce ATP for active transport of ions
Open stomata in light, close in dark/drought
In light: K⁺ ions pumped in → water follows by osmosis → cells become turgid → stoma opens
In dark/drought: K⁺ ions leave → water follows → cells become flaccid → stoma closes
Specialised cells can change back to unspecialised cells easily
In animals, differentiation is usually permanent. Only stem cells can differentiate into other cell types
Red blood cells have a nucleus but it's very small
Mature red blood cells in mammals have NO nucleus - it's ejected during development
Xylem cells are alive because they're in a living plant
Mature xylem vessels are dead - they're hollow tubes made of cell walls
Process by which cells become specialised for a function
Feature of a cell that helps it perform its function
Nerve cell that transmits electrical impulses
Long extension of a nerve cell that carries impulses
Protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen
Cap on sperm containing enzymes to penetrate the egg
Plant tissue that transports water upward
Pores in leaves controlled by guard cells
Differentiation is the process by which cells become specialised
Specialised cells have adaptations (structural features) suited to their function
Animal specialised cells include: nerve cells, red blood cells, sperm, egg, muscle cells, ciliated cells
Plant specialised cells include: root hair cells, xylem, phloem, palisade cells, guard cells
Each adaptation can be explained in terms of how it helps the cell perform its function
Structure and function are always linked in specialised cells
